    Print and summarise a SigDoTS result

    Source: R/print.R
    summary.sigdots.Rd

    print(fit) (or typing fit) shows the number of domains and the split tree of a sigdots() result. summary(fit) shows, in addition, the settings of the run and a table with one row per test; the table is also returned, as summary(fit)$tests, for use in your own code.

    Usage

    # S3 method for class 'sigdots'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'sigdots'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'summary.sigdots'
print(x, ...)

    Arguments

    x, object

    A result of sigdots() (for print.summary.sigdots(), a result of summary()).

    ...

    Not used.

    Value

    print() returns its argument invisibly. summary() returns a list of class "summary.sigdots" with two elements: fit, the result, and tests, the table described above (a data frame with the columns node, spots, candidate_domains, statistic, null_used, p_value, level and decision). Printing it shows the summary.

    Details

    The printed summary has four parts: the settings (header lines), the number of domains, the split tree, and the tests table, followed, where they apply, by the parts that could not be tested, the parts whose spots fall into separate pieces, and a note when the candidate domains were supplied by you.

    The header lines

    • Data: the number of spots and genes, and, for an object, where the expression came from.

    • Start: how the candidate domains were made (cluster_method, or "labels supplied by the user") and how many there are.

    • Spatial: the computation of the spatial covariance (Vecchia approximation with its number of neighbours, or exact).

    • Level: alpha, the significance level for the whole tree.

    • P-values: "Monte Carlo", or "normal approximation" with its numbers of simulated datasets (see pvalue_method in sigdots()).

    The split tree

    Every line that starts with a number in brackets, [9] say, is a part of the tree (a node): the number of spots it holds and the candidate domains it is made of, then the decision of the test at that node. SigDoTS tests from the top: the whole sample first, then the two sides of every split. split means the two sides are significantly different and each side is tested in turn; no split means they are not, and the part is a domain. => DOMAIN k marks a part that was not split further: it is the k-th domain, and the lines under it list the candidate domains it contains with their numbers of spots. A single candidate domain is never tested; when its parent is split, it is a domain by itself. [!] NOT TESTED marks a part that could not be tested because its spatial parameters could not be estimated; its spots get no domain. The tree is drawn with box-drawing characters, or with |-- and `-- where the console cannot show them.

    The tests table

    One row per part of the tree that the testing reached, from the top. The printed table shows the tested parts; the returned table, summary(fit)$tests, has every reached part, with NA numbers for those not tested. The columns:

    • node (printed as test): the node number used in the tree;

    • spots: the number of spots in that part;

    • candidate_domains: the candidate domains in that part (in the returned table only);

    • statistic: the split statistic of the data, between 0 and 1: the within-group sum of squares of the two sides of the split divided by the total sum of squares, over all genes. A smaller value means a clearer split;

    • null_used: the number of simulated single-domain datasets the test used;

    • p_value (printed as p): the p-value of the test. With the Monte Carlo p-value it is (1 + the number of simulated datasets whose statistic was at most the observed one) / (1 + null_used), so with few simulated datasets it can take only a few values; the decision is what the test establishes. With the normal approximation it is the normal probability of a statistic at most the observed one, given the mean and standard deviation of the simulated statistics; it is printed in scientific notation when below 0.0001;

    • level: the significance level of this test, alpha * (spots - 1) / (n - 1) for a sample of n spots, which keeps the probability of any false split in the whole tree at most alpha;

    • decision: split when p_value <= level, no split otherwise, or why the part was not tested: not tested: spatial fit (the spatial parameters could not be estimated because the part has too few spots; its spots get no domain), not tested: too few spots or not tested: a side too small (smaller than min_node_size or min_child_size of sigdots_control(); reported as a domain), not tested: B_cap too small (the level is so small that more than B_cap simulated datasets would be needed; reported as a domain).

    Separate pieces

    The tree needs the spots of each tested part to be connected through their nearest-neighbour links (k_nn of sigdots_control()). Where they fall into separate pieces (a layer cut by a fold of the tissue, or a few spots whose neighbours all belong to other candidate domains), SigDoTS joins each smaller piece to the rest by a link between their closest spots, repeatedly until all are connected, before it builds the trees of the data and of the simulated datasets. Nothing changes for parts whose spots are connected. summary() lists the parts where this happened, with the sizes of the pieces (for example "242, 49, 14 and 3 single spots").

    See also

    domains() for the domain of every spot, plot.sigdots() for the maps and the tree, sigdots() for the components of the result.

    Examples

    # \donttest{
fit <- sigdots(sigdots_example$x, sigdots_example$coords, K0 = 5, verbose = FALSE)
fit
#> SigDoTS: 900 spots, 200 genes
#> Number of domains: 3   (spots per domain: 300, 300, 300)
#> 
#> Split tree ([node] spots, candidate domains: decision):
#> [9] 900 spots, candidate domains 1,2,3,4,5: split
#> ├── [7] 300 spots, candidate domains 2,3: no split   => DOMAIN 1
#> │   ├── candidate domain 2  109 spots
#> │   └── candidate domain 3  191 spots
#> └── [8] 600 spots, candidate domains 1,4,5: split
#>     ├── [4] 300 spots, candidate domain 4   => DOMAIN 2
#>     └── [6] 300 spots, candidate domains 1,5: no split   => DOMAIN 3
#>         ├── candidate domain 1  103 spots
#>         └── candidate domain 5  197 spots
#> 
#> Use summary() for the tests.
summary(fit)
#> SigDoTS 0.2.5.8
#> Data:     900 spots x 200 genes
#> Start:    k-means on 15 principal components; 5 candidate domains
#> Spatial:  Vecchia approximation (60 neighbours)
#> Level:    0.05 for the whole tree
#> P-values: Monte Carlo
#> 
#> Number of domains: 3   (spots per domain: 300, 300, 300)
#> 
#> Split tree:
#> [9] 900 spots, candidate domains 1,2,3,4,5: split
#> ├── [7] 300 spots, candidate domains 2,3: no split   => DOMAIN 1
#> │   ├── candidate domain 2  109 spots
#> │   └── candidate domain 3  191 spots
#> └── [8] 600 spots, candidate domains 1,4,5: split
#>     ├── [4] 300 spots, candidate domain 4   => DOMAIN 2
#>     └── [6] 300 spots, candidate domains 1,5: no split   => DOMAIN 3
#>         ├── candidate domain 1  103 spots
#>         └── candidate domain 5  197 spots
#> 
#> Tests, from the top:
#>  test spots statistic null_used      p  level decision
#>   [9]   900     0.718        19 0.0500 0.0500    split
#>   [7]   300     0.935        10 0.2727 0.0166 no split
#>   [8]   600     0.903        30 0.0323 0.0333    split
#>   [6]   300     0.946        15 0.1250 0.0166 no split
summary(fit)$tests
#>   node spots candidate_domains statistic null_used    p_value      level
#> 1    9   900         1,2,3,4,5 0.7178312        19 0.05000000 0.05000000
#> 2    7   300               2,3 0.9345954        10 0.27272727 0.01662959
#> 3    8   600             1,4,5 0.9027189        30 0.03225806 0.03331479
#> 4    6   300               1,5 0.9464686        15 0.12500000 0.01662959
#>   decision
#> 1    split
#> 2 no split
#> 3    split
#> 4 no split
